#23237. Tech Report: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1549 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding love is major business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business.
  • In a recent development, the promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages.
  • As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this new generation of dating apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding love is major business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

In a recent development, the promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app people to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this new generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

So if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

What about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

According to recent reports, perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user states they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

If the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

What do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

Why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

Recent findings suggest that the truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

In a recent development, with the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

Recent findings suggest that an alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

Her research has been published in top academic journals as well as featured in popular news outlets such as The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Atlantic. She received her PhD in Social-Personality Psychology from UC Berkeley and her BA in Psychology from UCLA. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.
  • Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.
  • When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

“Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”.

Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:.

The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, neurodivergent kids aren’t the only ones who struggle with changing routines or new life phases. Adults can feel overwhelmed by transitions, too.

Whether starting a new job, moving to a new town, or sending a child off to college, transitions are equal parts exciting and uncomfortable for neurodivergent individuals.

The struggle often looks different in children and adults, but the demand is much the same: Stop what you are doing, shift your attention, figure out the next step, manage your emotions, and move into a different role, task, place, or expectation. The bigger the transition, the harder it feels.

Typical transitions include returning to work after a vacation, adjusting to a newly introduced schedule, shifting from work to parenting mode, navigating relationship changes, and recovering from illness or injury.

[Free Download: Get Control of Your Life and Schedule].

In a recent development, from the outside, the response of an adult with ADHD may look like procrastination, avoidance, irritability, disorganization, or poor follow-through. Internally, they are likely dealing with anxiety, emotional overload, decision fatigue, time blindness, or the frustration of knowing exactly what needs to be done but struggling to begin.

“I struggle so badly with transitions (they feel almost literally painful) that I spend up to five hours in a state of crippling inertia before handling a task that needs to be done,” wrote one woman with ADHD in a social media post, pleading for help.

In a recent development, transitions can be especially difficult when they involve uncertainty. A fresh job may bring excitement and anxiety about performance. A vacation may feel adventurous and overwhelming. Even a positive life change can feel unsettling when structure falls away.

“I don’t travel much,” notes Layla, an ADDitude reader from California. “Transitions are hard for me.”.

[Get This Free Download: Finish Your To-Do List Today].

Shave the rough edges off transitions by doing the following seven things:.

Most importantly, adults with ADHD should keep in mind that embracing change easily is not necessarily a sign of maturity. Feelings of anxiety around transitions may just mean that your brain needs more preview, structure, recovery, and support to move from one demand to the next.

60 mindful Upcoming Year's resolution ideas to try in 2027

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we’ve all been there.
  • Then two weeks later, on a Wednesday, you have the most stressful day at your job and you find yourself pouring a huge glass of wine.
  • Sources indicate that take a deep breath.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

According to recent reports, we’ve all been there. January 1st hits, and you decide this is the year you’re going to change your life and become the best version of yourself with some Latest Year’s resolutions. You might optimistically think, “You know what? I’m going to be healthier this year! I’m only going to drink on the weekends.”.

Then two weeks later, on a Wednesday, you have the most stressful day at your job and you find yourself pouring a huge glass of wine. You’re instantly filled with regret for breaking your resolution and vow to never do them again because they don’t work and are clearly designed to make you feel disappointed.

Sources indicate that take a deep breath. Resolutions don’t have to be this massive set up for failure that feel impossible to keep. They can be as big or as small as you want them to be. We’ve put together a list of 60 mindful resolutions that are less about striving for perfection or making huge changes in your life, and more about slowly helping you to grow and build better habits in an achievable way. Sounds nice, right?

So let’s ditch our list of impossible goals and jump into 60 resolutions that could help you thrive in 2027.

Industry observers note that at the end of the year, many of us step back and realize that we feel really disconnected from a lot of the people in our life. We get busy and stuck in our own little world. It’s too easy for connections with our family, friends, partners, or coworkers to dwindle from time to time.

It has been revealed that if this sounds familiar, here are 15 resolutions that can help you build more fulfilling relationships so that your support networks are there for you when you need it. (And you’re there for them when they need it too.).

Sources indicate that pro tip: you don’t need to do all of 15. Just try choosing a few that feel good to you and then take some small steps towards adding them into your routine.

Make a habit of giving your full attention to the people who matter most to you. Try planning regular (or semi-regular) family dinners, date nights, or hangs with friends. If you like phone calls, those work great too. (Just make sure you’re fully present!).

Industry observers note that when someone’s talking to you, focus fully on what they’re saying instead of thinking about your reply or what you’re going to eat for your next meal (we’ve all been there). Active listening demonstrates respect to your loved one and can help deepen your bond. If you want to get better at active listening, here are eight techniques to help.

Too often, we take those around us for granted, so let the people in your life know you appreciate them. Saying something as easy as, “thank you” or writing a cute little note can let your loved one know how much they mean to you and make them feel good. Who doesn’t want to make their loved one feel good?

If you love them, say it. Life’s too short! Telling someone you love them is powerful and can help you grow a stronger bond. If you have people in your life like a macho uncle or disengaged cousin who have a hard time saying I love you, be the first to jump in and show them that it’s okay to express your affection for one another.

Sources indicate that if you notice someone struggling in your life, step in and help. It doesn't need to be revolutionary. It could be helping with laundry or simply being there to listen. Just letting them know that you see their efforts and want to help can make a huge difference.

Relationships are work. And in order for them to work, you need to put time into them. So set a reminder to check in with your loved ones, especially the ones you don’t see often. A quick text or call can do the trick and help you stay connected with your favorite people. And if you have folks in your life who are struggling, or who experience loneliness, make an extra effort to reach out and show you care.

Don’t let misunderstandings grow. When you’re upset with someone, bring it up to them calmly and kindly, and with the goal of finding a solution. It can help to lead with “I feel” statements. And if your feelings are hurt over an innocent misunderstanding, start with, “I know you didn’t mean to hurt my feelings but,” so the other person knows they’re not in trouble and you want to come to a place of understanding.

This might sound obvious, but if your loved one has good news, show genuine excitement for the good things that are happening for them. We all feel good when others celebrate with us. So send those flowers — almost no one’s going to get mad at you for sending flowers. Sometimes celebrating success for others feels hard if you feel stuck in your life, but by genuinely finding happiness for others, you may feel the glow of that happiness yourself.

Use conversions with others as a time to genuinely disconnect from technology and focus on being together. When you’re spending time with someone, keep your phone in your pocket, in your purse, or somewhere that’s not in your hand. Give your loved one your full attention. This will make them feel seen and it helps you to stay more in the moment and form deeper connections.

Everyone loves to feel seen and valued. Sometimes just surprising someone you love with a small gesture can make their day. It doesn’t have to be substantial, it could just be showing up to a hang with your loved one’s favorite snack, their preferred coffee drink, or even a small bouquet of flowers. Trying to be better about budgeting? Handwritten cards, or homemade crafts also make lovely surprises.

According to recent reports, when someone you care about is struggling, before reacting, take a moment to put yourself in their shoes and understand what they might be going through. This can be a lot easier remarked than done, but try to treat them the way you would want to be treated —  with kindness instead of judgment.

💙 If Empathy doesn’t come easy for you, check out this meditation from Tamara Levitt’s Relationships with Others series.

We all have preferences for how we like to give and receive love and it’s so special when the people in our lives make an effort to communicate affection in the ways we most appreciate. So take some time to understand a partner, family member, or friends love languages (here’s an overview of all five and how to identify yours). Showing love in the ways they like can make you closer. (And probably earn you brownie points!).

Recent findings suggest that say yes to an invite or an activity you wouldn’t normally do. Stepping out of your comfort zone can help you feel energized and open you up to fresh experiences and learnings about yourself. The one time when it’s okay not to say yes is if you’re establishing boundaries with your emotional energy or time. It’s all about balance!

While saying yes is great (see above), saying no is also important. Make an effort to have healthy relationships with solid boundaries. Tell people what you need, like alone time or limits on work talk. And respect their boundaries too. If all of that sounds tough, check out these six tips to setting healthy boundaries in your relationships.

Recent findings suggest that humans make mistakes and the best thing you can do is to acknowledge them, learn and grow. So try to take responsibility if you make a mistake. You’ll feel free of guilt and you won’t have to double down on something you probably didn’t mean to do in the first place (like a bad joke that hurt someone’s feelings, or a meeting you were super late for.) A heartfelt apology can mend any damage and show your maturity (these seven tips will help you do it).

It has been revealed that doesn’t it feel like we’re always trying to find a better work-life balance, get promoted, improve our work ethic, and feel more fulfilled with the work we’re doing? That constant desire for some sort of growth or change can be overwhelming and leave you not knowing where to start.

So we’ve put together 15 work resolutions that might be more sustainable and rewarding for you — and will hopefully make the whole process feel less overwhelming.

Industry observers note that protecting your personal time is so key for avoiding burnout, so decide on clear work hours and stick to them. Try setting a goal for logging off by 6pm or not looking at emails in your off time. If your job doesn’t right now give you the freedom to set these boundaries, chat with your superiors and express your goals where work-life balance is concerned.

Organize your workspace to reduce clutter. A working area that you like (or at least doesn’t cause more stress) can really improve your mood and your focus. Once you reduce the clutter and get rid of any items that aren’t sparking joy, you could mindfully add things that feel good like a plant, photo, or a comfy chair.

In a recent development, large projects can be overwhelming. Try breaking them down into smaller, more manageable steps to make them less daunting and help you stay on track. You can also practice time-boxing to keep your focus — here’s how to do it .

According to recent reports, go for a five-minute walk, enjoy a cup or tea, or do a quick stretch. It doesn’t really matter what you do on a break, just that you do something to rest your mind and give your body a little love. Set reminders if it’ll help you remember. (Here are 20 ways to take a mindful break.).

Recent findings suggest that start each day by identifying your top three priorities. If you focus on the most important tasks first, this will help you make progress where it matters most. Got a few things on your to-do list that aren’t time sensitive? Resist the temptation to try to get them done when you’re exhausted and bump them to tomorrow when you can focus.

According to recent reports, just like you want to celebrate the achievements of the people in your life, it’s equally important to celebrate yourself! Take note of all of your accomplishments. This can help boost your confidence, help you stay motivated, and even make you smile.

In a recent development, making new friends isn’t just for your school years. Make an effort to connect with coworkers or other people in your field. Getting coffee with colleagues can help you build relationships and even help with career growth. You might find that your career is more fulfilling when you have solid relationships with colleagues and coworkers.

In a recent development, work on being clear and concise in emails, meetings, and in conversations. Practicing good communication not only improves your productivity but also helps avoid misunderstandings (these 13 tips can help).

Recent findings suggest that if you’re overwhelmed and juggling too much, look for tasks that can be given to others to make your life easier. This doesn’t mean you’re not good at your job. It just means you're making sure your energy is spent where it’s needed most.

Struggling to focus? Single-tasting is where it’s at. Take on one task at a time and not five at once. This will improve the quality of your work and help you feel less like you want to scream.

According to recent reports, even if it’s scary, seek out feedback from your boss, coworkers, or clients. Constructive input can help you get better and show that you want to improve. Just make sure you’re also receiving feedback for things you’re doing well, not just areas where you could do better.

Sources indicate that find a method that helps you stay on top of deadlines. A to-do list app, a daily planner, or a bullet journal could help keep track of all your tasks. Explore some different ideas to find what works best for you.

Sources indicate that don’t hesitate to ask for what you need. If anything, this can help you get taken more seriously and help with career growth. Ask for that raise, request that more flexible schedule, tell your boss you need additional resources to complete that project.

💙 Learn how to practice Speaking Up at work with this session from the Mindful Leadership Wisdom Series.

In a recent development, set goals that align with your long-term dreams and values, not just what you hope to achieve. These could be around building confidence, becoming a more mindful leader, or exploring a new field you’ve always been interested in.

In a recent development, when you don’t feel mentally like you’re firing on all cylinders, it can be tough to even think of what to focus on to help your mental health. We get it — you’re probably already stressed, so making a decision on a resolution to be less stressed might be the last thing you want to (or can) do.

To help you out, we put together a list of 15 small and intentional resolutions that will help nurture your mind and create space for calm and joy in 2027.

Industry observers note that (Psst: You don’t have to do all of them. Start with one or two that’ll help you feel more balanced, calm, and connected, and then go from there.).

In a recent development, write down and reflect on your thoughts, feelings, and experiences each day. This can help you process your emotions and recognize some patterns you have. Journaling is also a great way to practice gratitude.

Industry observers note that each day, take a moment to think of three things you’re grateful for. This can rewire your brain to look for the positives in your life. It doesn’t have to be getting a promotion or finding your perfect partner, it can be as small as not burning your bagel today. If you want to find more ways to incorporate gratitude into your days, here are eight ideas to get you started.

Sources indicate that spend a few minutes a day practicing mindfulness. And while this could be a five minute meditation, it could also be a bit of deep breathing on a work break, or just noticing the sights and sounds on your morning walk. Any moment where you become fully present counts!

Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day to help you get better quality sleep (here are six more tips to help you get those Zzzzs). The more rested you are, the more you’ll be able to handle the stress that comes up throughout the day.

Nature has a way of calming us down and recharging us, so if it’s possible, try to get outside everyday. It doesn't have to be a big hike, it can be as simple as walking around your block or even just going into your yard.

Recent findings suggest that this is a big one! Try to gradually reduce the time you spend on your phone, computer, or watching TV, especially before bed. You could read that novel that’s been on your bedside table for ever or catch up with a loved one instead. But take it slow, we know it’s not easy.

Give yourself permission to say no to things that overwhelm or overcommit you. It’s more vital to protect your energy than to burn yourself out trying to please other people. If saying no is hard for you, here’s 30 ways to do it nicely.

Get in the habit of reaching out to a loved one or a therapist when you’re feeling stressed or overwhelmed. Talking about our feelings can help us feel lighter and even give us a latest perspective.

A clean environment isn’t just for your desk. Having a clean home can calm you too. So take some small steps to organize your home. You might try doing just one room at a time, it doesn’t need to be all at once.

Schedule regular breaks so you don’t have a meltdown. These pauses can really help you reduce your stress and keep you focused. Grabbing a glass of water, breathing deeply, or gently stretching can all help reset you and give your mind a moment to rest.

Treat yourself the way you would your closest friend. Avoid going in on yourself with harsh, critical thoughts and instead say some sweet nothings to yourself. We know this isn’t always easy, so here are eight tips to help you quiet that inner critic.

In a recent development, start a hobby that lets you express yourself. This can be therapeutic and put you in a better mood. Ever been curious about painting or playing music? Maybe now’s your chance to explore that curiosity.

Exercising relieves a lot of stress. But you don’t need to spend hours at the gym or set some massive weight loss goal. Instead, try out a fresh yoga class, have a dance party in your living room, or find other ways to move your body that feel nourishing to you.

Go easy on yourself, you don’t need to be perfect (newsflash: there’s no such thing). It can help to focus on all the small ways you're growing each day, not on the destination. Sometimes it’s better to think about growth-setting instead of goal setting.

In a recent development, don’t regularly spend your time on something that drains your energy. Seek out places that bring you positivity instead. If certain people you hang around with make you feel bad, limit your exposure to them. This might look like setting boundaries with family about how many events you attend each year, or with friends by limiting how much you talk or get together.

💙 If you’re looking for more positivity in your life, learn how to Process and Move Past Negativity during the Overcome Stress and Anxiety series with Dr. Julie Smith.

Okay, let’s face it. Most of us want to look and feel our best — and there’s nothing wrong with that. But better physical health is also about feeling energized, staying strong, and giving our body the help it needs to thrive.

We don’t need to tell you that working out consistently is a lot easier mentioned than done. Sure, in a perfect world, we always have the time and energy to get to the gym. But we don’t live in that world. We have endless responsibilities and working out might be the first thing to go when we’re busy.

According to recent reports, so explore these 15 manageable resolutions that can help you feel strong and energized going into 2027. And remember, you don’t need to force yourself to go all-in on physical wellness to feel better. Just start with one or two that feel like they’d be easier to make a consistent habit and go from there.

In a recent development, aim for some form of movement every day –– it doesn’t have to be intense. Try a 10–minute stretch or a brisk walk through your favorite part of your neighborhood. Focus on what makes you feel good in your body, which may change day to day.

Industry observers note that hydration makes you feel good and stay alert, so try to aim for 8–10 glasses of water a day. Carry a reusable water bottle with you to make it easier to hit your goal and remind you to drink. If regular water feels boring try adding slices of your favorite citrus or fresh mint to your water.

It has been revealed that add a rainbow of foods to your plate! Focus on eating a mix of fruits, veggies, lean proteins, and whole grains. Try meal prepping ahead of time to make it easier for you to choose healthy options. Bonus points if you try to stay mindful while you cook and while you eat — here’s how.

Sources indicate that swap out processed snacks for healthier options like fruit, nuts, seeds, or yogurt. Try keeping nutritious snacks nearby to make it easier to avoid reaching your favorite sweets. With that in mind, don’t forget that dark chocolate has some antioxidants so adding a few dark chocolate chips to your trail mix is a-okay with us!

When you sleep better, you feel better. End of story. Aim for around eight hours of quality sleep each night. It can help to have a wind down routine at the end of your day to help your body know that it’s time for rest. These nine steps can help you create a calming bedtime routine.

In a recent development, if you are able to take stairs instead of elevators or escalators, go for it! Making small, active choices throughout your day to help you get a little more movement. You could also try parking farther away to get in a few extra steps.

Sources indicate that add some stretching into your daily routine to improve your flexibility, reduce your tension, and prevent injuring yourself. Try stretching for a few minutes as soon as you get out of bed or right before you get into bed — here are seven we like.

Recent findings suggest that we know it can be frustrating or scary to go see a doctor, but don’t wait to see one until you feel sick. Set up your physicals and dental cleanings so that you can breathe easy and not worry about your health. You’ll be proud of yourself when you leave that doctor’s office!

Generally, it’s recommended to cut back on foods high in sugar. You may be surprised how much sugar some of your daily go-tos have, so stay mindful of what you’re consuming (you could check the labels for sugar content if that works for you).. It’s not about never having a treat, but bringing more awareness to what you’re eating and how it’s making you feel. It’s all about balance.

Working out can really feel like work a lot of the time. So shake up your routine to help keep you excited to exercise. Ever tried kickboxing or swimming? Maybe 2027 is the year you hop in the boxing ring or jump in the pool.

If you have a desk job, try to stand up and move every hour. Consider switching to a standing desk if that’s an option. If you work from home and have space for a walking pad in front of a standing desk you can also get your steps in while you work.

In a recent development, we know that the new year isn’t always the time you want to get outside for a walk, but sunshine and time in nature can boost your mood. If you live in the northern hemisphere, bundle up and try going for a walk, run, or bike ride outside whenever the weather allows it.

In a recent development, if you drink alcohol, consider cutting back by a few drinks or setting limits. It can help to have fun or festive swap, so try sipping on flavored sparkling water or a mocktail at a social event or as a treat at the end of a long week. Sometimes creating a special drink that’s free of booze creates the same excitement as making a special cocktail. And you might love the way you feel the next morning when you’re hydrating your body with your evening beverage instead of dehydrating it.

It has been revealed that good posture helps prevent back and neck pain so pay attention to how you sit and stand. And add exercises that focus on strengthening your core into your workout. This will help support better alignment. Sitting at a desk for work? Set alarms every so often to remind you to stand up and stretch.

Celebrating your progress helps you to keep going — we all need a good pat on the back. If you drink an extra glass of water or walk an extra mile, take note of it. Maybe even do a little happy dance. If you go for a walk four days in a row, make a note in your journal or notebook. The more you celebrate your progress the prouder of yourself you’ll be (and the easier it is to keep it up).

💙 Learn how to celebrate the Small Wins on the path to achieving your larger goals with help from Jay Shetty.

Fresh Year’s resolutions are personal goals or promises you make to yourself at the start of a new year. They can be about anything and it’s entirely up to you. They can be big like training for a marathon or small like drinking more water.

Sources indicate that usually people use it as a chance to reflect, change up some patterns in their life, and start fresh. If you’re looking to set a resolution but don’t know where to start, here are five areas people tend to focus on:.

Industry observers note that you don’t have to make resolutions to have a wonderful new year. But if you want to try, keep in mind that resolutions work best when you make them work for you. So yes — resolutions matter if you use them as a tool to help you live with more purpose and joy, then you’ll set yourself up for more success.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re setting your resolutions, focus on what would make you feel happier, healthier and more fulfilled and go from there. And approach resolutions with kindness and flexibility, especially if you don’t end up following through on one.

Recent findings suggest that if the idea of resolutions feels overwhelming — we get it. Here’s three ways that could make it easier for you:.

Focus on one word or theme for the year that feels right to you, like “balance” or “growth.”.

Set a small monthly intention instead of a year-long commitment.

Celebrate progress instead of perfection by noticing little wins along the way.

According to recent reports, we wish there were five magical resolutions that could solve all of our problems at once. But unfortunately there’s no such thing. What we can tell you is the most successful resolutions tend to be the ones that feel right to you.

Recent findings suggest that it’s important to focus on the right area when setting your resolution, so you’ll be more likely to stick with them. Here are five areas to focus on when setting your resolution:.

Resolutions that focus on building stronger relationships — Pick ones that’ll fill you up and add more joy to your life.

Resolutions that focus on taking care of your physical health — Pick ones that focus on regular exercise, better nutrition, or improved sleep.

Resolutions that focus on your mental health — Pick ones that practice gratitude or mindfulness, so that they can help you feel calmer and more balanced.

Resolutions that focus on your career –– Pick ones that focus on learning a new skill or creating a better work-life balance so that your professional life can become more rewarding.

Resolutions that focus on personal growth –– Pick ones that focus on starting newly introduced hobbies or giving back to your community.

Sources indicate that all of us at one point or another have probably failed at a resolution we’ve set for ourselves. And when that happens, it can feel pretty disappointing. But resolutions can work — if you set them in the right way.

It has been revealed that resolutions that are vague or overly ambitious tend to be a recipe for failure. But if you set ones that are realistic and meaningful to you, it’ll be a lot easier to keep your resolution and see the change you want. But remember to be flexible and kind to yourself. We’re all not perfect and mistakes happen. So try not to beat yourself up if you don’t stick to your goals perfectly. Focus on progress, not perfection.

In a recent development, if you find it easier to set monthly intentions as opposed to setting one year-long resolution, go for that. Tailor the resolutions so they work best for you.

Sometimes the minute we think of resolutions, we can get sad or overwhelmed at the baggage of our past failed resolutions. If this is you — we understand. Resolutions aren’t for everyone. But if you’re interested, there are other ways you can focus on self-improvement and growth.

It has been revealed that if a long list of goals is too daunting for you, try picking a single word to guide your year. You could use words like “balance,” or “connection,” to remind yourself to make choices that match with your values.

If setting smaller, short-term goals might help you to stay motivated, you could try focusing on building better sleep habits in January, and then shifting to something like improving your diet in February.

It has been revealed that if tracking your progress will make it more fun for you and help you to invest more, try using a habit tracker app, or even just a calendar. This way it’ll be easier to celebrate your little wins along the way.

According to recent reports, resolutions that focus on relationships can bring more connection, understanding, and happiness into your life. And a good way to show the people you love the most how much they mean to you is to set a resolution to spend more quality time with them.

Acts of kindness also go a long way to strengthen your relationships. So if this is vital to you, try setting an intention to express gratitude more often, like thanking your partner for their support.

You could also set a resolution to unplug more often. This can help free up your time and create more meaningful, distraction-free moments with the people you care about the most.

#23232. Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles.
  • According to recent reports, that’s just your teens becoming independent.
  • Industry observers note that none of this is easy, of course.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles. In the teen years, sweet hugs can provoke eye rolls; a well-intentioned “How was your day?” may be misconstrued as meddling.

According to recent reports, that’s just your teens becoming independent. Decades of research finds that portraying adolescence as a period of “storm and stress” is not only misguided, it’s harmful. In fact, developmental science shows this time of life is better recast as “the breakthrough years.” According to research on over one thousand adolescents by Ellen Galinsky, author and president of Families and Work Institute, there are key messages that teens want to get through to adults:.

Industry observers note that none of this is easy, of course. Along the way, tough situations crop up, and it’s hard to know what to do. Here are common questions, with answers backed by scientists and their research.

In a recent development, Q: My 16-year-old doesn’t seem to be motivated to do anything beyond hanging out with friends and playing video games. When I bring up the prospect of college, he indicates he doesn’t care. What should I do?

It has been revealed that A: As parents, we want to set our high schoolers up for success. But, at that age, young people are still trying to figure out who they are, what interests them, and what their future looks like. “Identity development and purpose formation are underway, but rarely fully formed by high school,” indicates Kendall Cotton Bronk, professor of psychology at Claremont Graduate University.

Recent findings suggest that not finding any answers yet is expected. “Parents need to remind themselves that where their child is at this moment in time isn’t necessarily where they will be in the future,” says Bronk.

To help teens along, encourage them to try different activities at school and in the community, whether it’s, for instance, robotics, the debate team, chorus, improv, or the school paper. Leave it to them to select what to try. Don’t do it for them. Don’t judge their choices.

Industry observers note that “While it’s not appropriate for parents to be too directive, they can help their teenager reflect on what they liked and didn’t like and what felt meaningful and not so meaningful about their various experiences,” claims Bronk. “Having someone to debrief with can help them deepen their reflection and more swiftly identify a purposeful direction.”.

According to recent reports, research suggests that when teens are guided by their own interests, free of external pressures, they’re more likely to take charge of their own career development. But when parents are overly involved in their adolescents’ lives, notes Bronk, young people don’t have an opportunity to cultivate a sense of agency, and this can make career development planning a big challenge.

Industry observers note that instead of trying to manage their path, notes Bronk, parents should simply “be curious.” Ask your child: What interests you? What feels satisfying for you?

“This kind of questioning can scaffold and deepen their young person’s reflections, and reflection is a key component of figuring out what kind of path a young person wants to follow,” she indicates. “Usually, what holds their interest is something they’re good at and care about, and that allows them to make a meaningful difference in the broader world,” she explains.

Taking advantage of volunteer opportunities can help young people see themselves as useful and discover careers that might interest them—for instance, helping out in a food pantry, animal shelter, a kids sports organization, or hospital. Encourage your teen to ask people he knows about their jobs, what they entail, and what they studied to get there.

In a recent development, finally, don’t assume that your child’s lack of direction is apathy. Whatever their interest is, “work with it, not against it,” notes Bronk. “At the same time, be patient. It may just be the case that they haven’t figured it all out yet. Their timetable may not be the same as yours, but they will eventually get there. Remember, this isn’t a race.”.

Q: My 15-year-old seems to be living a separate life. He spends most of his time in his room and has dinner more often with his friends than with us. How can we encourage him to be a part of the family?

A: Seeking independence (while still navigating being dependent on adults) is one of the primary tasks of adolescents as they transition to becoming more self-sufficient into early adulthood.

According to recent reports, “I try to get parents to understand that it’s not about them,” says Laurence Steinberg, author of You and Your Adolescent. “The parents didn’t do anything wrong; the child isn’t rejecting them. This is a sign they’re growing up normally. It’s partly wanting to make their own decisions and have their own life, but it’s also wanting emotional independence—to show that they are more than their parents’ kid.”.

Chances are a closed door doesn’t mean trouble. Just as most adults don’t want others listening in on their calls, teens don’t want that either. They’re not distancing themselves from you, but simply distancing themselves from being a child.

“There’s nothing the parents can do to stop this from happening,” indicates Steinberg, a professor emeritus of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University. “And they shouldn’t try.”.

That said, spending time with family is also key. To suggest that, say something like, “We want to spend more time with you, but we also know that spending time with friends is important. What’s the best way to catch up with you?” By making the planning of it a collaborative process, your child is more likely to stay engaged. Research suggests that they may even find the activity more enjoyable.

Only rarely is a shut bedroom door cause for concern—for instance, you notice other behavioral changes, such as a drop in grades, a dwindling interest in his usual in-person activities. If you suspect an glitch, let your child know that you’re there for him, and that he can get professional help, too.

One last note: If your child is spending most of his time in his room online, setting limits on its own may not be enough, says Jacqueline Nesi, author of the Techno Sapiens newsletter and associate professor of psychiatry and human behavior at Brown University. You’ll also want to discuss with them what you want for him and what he wants.

Recent findings suggest that the evidence also supports “co-viewing” or “co-using” technology with your kids, whether that’s a video game, TV, or an AI chatbot, says Nesi. Using tech together can spark conversation and help parents better understand their kids’ digital lives.

It has been revealed that that stated, it’s still important for you to protect their sleep and to make sure that they live a life in person. Again, to get their buy-in, decide on screen-time parameters, and replace screen time with in-person activities he might enjoy, such cooking a favorite meal together or an outing with family and friends.

Industry observers note that Q: My 17-year-old daughter recently suffered a breakup. How can I help her feel better without intruding?

Industry observers note that A: Even if a relationship doesn’t look like a monogamous romantic relationship in adulthood (it may be short, or the partners may not talk to each other very much), these breakups can still be painful. So always take your teen’s romantic activities seriously, as well as the emotions they are experiencing following a breakup, indicates Emily Bibby, a researcher at the Relationship Development Center at Stony Brook University. Be compassionate, validating, and nonjudgmental. Let her know that she is having a normal reaction to a difficult situation.

Allow space to grieve and vent. “Listen hard to what your child is thinking and feeling,” says Barry Farber, professor of psychology and education at Columbia University Teachers College. “Ask what they’ve learned from the relationship. Framing the relationship as a learning experience, as opposed to a failure, can help nurture resilience and personal growth, and can help her feel more in control and more hopeful about future relationships.”.

As Farber and his coauthors point out in a recent study, while time doesn’t necessarily “heal all wounds” (because memories and thoughts can linger), it almost always “softens the blow” when other strategies are also employed, such as talking with a trusted friend or family member. While the study involved mostly white, female adult subjects, the same principle generally applies across ages, genders, and ethnicities. Letting your child know that things will get better can help.

Trying to convince a teen to do anything is difficult, states Farber, so it’s better to simply listen, and then only encourage as opposed to insisting or dictating. Encourage her to engage in activities she enjoys, whether it’s treating herself to an afternoon manicure, going to a concert, or spending time in nature like hiking and walking on the beach. Encourage her to avoid all contact with her ex, both in person and on social media. If one person believes it’s really over, a clean break is usually best, says Farber. Any surge of adrenaline that happens when you see your ex in any form is only temporary, and only makes it harder to get over the breakup.

If sad feelings are impairing day-to-day life—she’s not seeing friends, she’s failing her classes, there’s a dramatic change in eating or sleeping—have her consider seeking help from a mental health professional. “Therapy normalizes the experience,” notes Farber. “It helps people find a latest narrative when they’re stuck.”.

Therapy also gives people an opportunity to share their feelings in a private space and learn evidence-based emotion-regulation skills to improve their mental health and functioning, notes Bibby.

This workbook is for a range of practitioners who support parents and caregivers of children between preschool and high school.

If your teen is debilitatingly depressed or harming herself, then advise that she get professional help as soon as possible, such as from her school psychologist, her primary care doctor (for a referral), or a therapist you think highly of.

It has been revealed that to help their teen navigate relationships in general, parents can model healthy relationships with not just a partner, but also friends and family members. Teaching your teen effective communication skills and boundary setting early on, in the context of friendships and family relationships, can prove helpful once your teen starts dating, indicates Bibby, who recently coauthored a research review on romantic relationships and mental health in adolescents.

And as for parents of teens who are just becoming interested in dating, it’s helpful to talk about what healthy relationships look like, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect. “Thinking through what they would do [in different dating scenarios] and how to navigate different challenges that may arise can build confidence when they start dating,” indicates Bibby.

Q: My 14-year-old has found herself in a friend group that spends a lot of money on expensive clothing and electronics. We don’t approve of these teens and don’t share their consumerist values. How do we prevent our child from becoming materialistic, too?

A: You can empower your teen to make thoughtful, confident choices about money, friendships, and the pressures they face. Try leading with connection rather than control: Talk openly about your family’s values, help them practice setting boundaries, and remind them they do not need to match their friends’ spending to belong or feel worthy. Expensive tastes and social media pressures can be hard to ignore, but your teen can learn to make choices that reflect what matters most to them.

Recent findings suggest that people turn to materialistic things to fill a void, but that’s only a temporary fix, notes Lan Nguyen Chaplin, a professor of integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University, and an expert in children’s and teens’ consumer behavior. “They end up in a vicious cycle of wanting and needing more to fill the same void because material things cannot fill real voids.”.

In her research exploring materialism in a group of 12- to 18-year-olds, she reported that those with high self-esteem were less likely to have materialistic tendencies. “Parents and peers [are] a source of emotional support and psychological well-being,” she writes. “Supportive parents and peers boost adolescents’ self-esteem, which decreases their need to turn to material goods to develop positive self-perceptions.”.

According to recent reports, read this article in Spanish on La Red Hispana, the public-facing media outlet and distribution house of HCN, focused on educating, inspiring, and informing 40 million U.S. Hispanics.

According to recent reports, to that end, start at home and help your kids feel good about themselves. Gratitude journals can be a good way to curb materialism, but, of course, asking a teen who is new to journaling to start one can feel like a homework writing assignment if it’s yet another thing they are required to do. Rather, approach it with a light touch. Model gratitude by sharing with your teen who and what you’re grateful for, keep a gratitude journal yourself, or ask them what the high point of their day is.

It also helps to stop tying accomplishments to material things. So, instead of, say, rewarding a good report card with money or sneakers, celebrate the hard work that was put into achieving the good grades over a fun experience together like a movie night at home.

Most of all, spend time with your teen in lighthearted and playful ways, no matter how short. Even a 10-minute car ride can be a good opportunity to connect with them, and also reinforce the good things they have going for them, Chaplin indicates.

Joanne Chen is a writer and editor in New York City. Her articles on children and parenting have appeared in The Bump, Parents Magazine, and the New York Times.

ADHD in Midlife & Beyond: 5 Big Research Findings

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.
  • The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.
  • An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.

The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.

An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records. Missed diagnoses and misdiagnoses make research on this population difficult — but not impossible.

Amber John, Ph.D., a researcher at the University of Liverpool, reviewed studies on how the experience of ADHD changes with age during her November 2026 ADDitude webinar, “Aging with ADHD: Upcoming Research Findings in Midlife and Beyond.”.

Below are some of the themes John highlighted and what they suggest about the support adults with ADHD need in midlife and beyond.

Industry observers note that in clinical interviews, adults with ADHD recalled feeling different growing up but being unable to explain why. A diagnosis helped them see those experiences in a different light.

“These experiences that previously might have seemed disconnected, for many, started to form this more understandable pattern,” John said. “And that could really change the meaning that someone gives to those past experiences, particularly where they had just been viewed as evidence of personal failings.”.

[Read: The Transformative Power of an ADHD Diagnosis for Older Women].

Many people with ADHD develop painstaking routines and coping strategies to manage symptoms. The effort it takes to keep those routines going often goes unseen and can fuel burnout.

“This raises a really key question about what it is that we actually mean when we say someone is functioning well,” John said. “Understanding someone’s support needs really means that we need to ask about the cost of managing.”.

The experience of ADHD changes as life circumstances change. Menopause, caring for aging parents, and retirement can affect how symptoms play out in daily life and disrupt routines that have helped people cope for decades.

“A way that somebody is using to manage or to cope that’s worked in one period of life might become less useful when health, or demands, or available support changes,” John stated.

According to recent reports, [Read: I Feared I Had Alzheimer’s. It Turns Out It Was Undiagnosed ADHD.].

In doctors’ offices and workplaces, people with ADHD often shoulder the burden of explaining their needs and advocating for basic support. They can put considerable effort into managing their symptoms and still face barriers to getting care or participating at work.

“There is a limit to focusing on individual-level coping because a person can put really substantial effort into managing whilst the environment actually continues to make participation difficult,” John said.

It has been revealed that john’s research highlights the need for ADHD support that adapts as people’s circumstances change. We shouldn’t assume that “what helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s,” she said.

For more on ADHD in midlife and beyond, watch the full webinar at additu.de/111726.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you open the app store to look for a meditation app and find dozens of options promising calmer days, deeper sleep, less stress, and sharper focus. It’s hard to know where to start or which claims to believe.

Below, we cover three well-known meditation apps: Calm, Headspace, and Insight Timer. We've looked at what each one offers and named what we like about it, so you can decide which one to try.

In a recent development, before we dive in, a quick note on where we’re coming from. We make Calm, and we love it. We hope you will too, but another option might suit you better.

In a recent development, the best meditation app for you depends on what you’re looking for. To narrow it down, ask yourself these questions:.

What do you want help with? Maybe it’s stress relief, better sleep, sharper focus, or a guided start as a beginner.

How much variety do you need? Some people want an extensive library to explore, while others prefer a smaller collection built around a specific goal.

It has been revealed that how personal do you want it to feel? You might prefer an app that tailors recommendations to your mood and goals, or one that leaves the choosing to you.

According to recent reports, what's your budget? Compare what the free and paid tiers include, since a generous free version may be all you need.

Calm is one of the most widely used meditation apps, and it also offers sleep content, music, gentle movement sessions, and more. People use Calm at night for sleep and during the day for stress.

According to recent reports, content library: The app features Sleep Stories, bedtime tales read by well-known voices, alongside daily meditation programs including the flagship Daily Calm. You'll also find breathwork exercises, mindful tools, soundscapes, intro courses, and longer programs on themes like anxiety and self-kindness.

Sources indicate that personalization: Calm’s Check-Ins let you log your mood, sleep, and gratitude, so you can spot patterns over time. You can set reminders and follow a series of sessions to build a routine.

As People Live Longer, How Can We Live Better?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when the Stanford Center on Longevity launched in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions.
  • Recent findings suggest that another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging.
  • In a recent development, in 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center rolled out the Latest Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when the Stanford Center on Longevity launched in 2007, founding director Laura Carstensen spent a lot of time correcting misperceptions. “The initial response people had was, ‘Like the Methuselah Foundation? You are going to extend life?’” Carstensen was clear that the center’s aim was not to increase lifespans—which had nearly doubled during the 20th century—but rather to build societies that accommodated that upcoming and unprecedented reality.

Recent findings suggest that another persistent misperception was that “longevity” is a euphemism for aging and that the Stanford Center on Longevity was a center on aging. As Carstensen noted often, “Longevity is not synonymous with aging. It is a metric of length.” The center’s interest is in the challenges and opportunities that longer lives present. While the center is keenly interested in older people, in Carstensen’s view, “longer lives have implications for every stage of life, and the roots of many problems faced at advanced ages have their roots much earlier in life.” The center’s mission is to use longer lives to improve quality of life at all ages.

In a recent development, in 2019, under Carstensen’s leadership, the center rolled out the Latest Map of Life initiative, designed to rethink the human life course in response to skyrocketing life expectancies, and it has trained nearly 40 postdoctoral fellows, mentored by faculty affiliates spanning multiple disciplines, about the ways in which longevity is transforming societies, cultures, and economies. After nearly 20 years, Carstensen, the Fairleigh S. Dickinson Jr. Professor in Public Policy and a professor of psychology at Stanford, will step down this summer from her role at the Stanford Center on Longevity to pursue a new project alongside her research and teaching.

Sources indicate that I spoke with Carstensen about what she’s learned along the way and what’s next. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Karen Breslau: What’s changed since the center’s early days?

Laura Carstensen: I hope it’s clearer that the aging process has not changed much, if any, genetically over the last several thousand years. Rather, longevity—the length of life—increased, and that has enormous implications for nearly all aspects of our lives. The modifiability of aging, on the other hand, is also clear. Even though we’re essentially the same physiological beings that our ancestors were, we changed the world in ways that are allowing us to live healthier and longer. That’s why we are confident that we can build a world where the majority of people live well for a century.

Recent findings suggest that KB: You are on the scientific advisory council to the Health District of Singapore, which is building the Queenstown Health District, a very intentional all-ages community that is incorporating principles from the Upcoming Map of Life. What are you seeing?

LC: The Singapore government has given a group of scientists the freedom to design a neighborhood in ways that support long-term health and intergenerational connections, continued financial security, and exercise. They’re thinking about all the factors that contribute to long, healthy, and engaged lives and literally programming them into the community. What’s really cool about the Queenstown Health District is that it can provide a proof of concept that social and physical designs can improve long life.

Already they have built parks and playgrounds with swings for the kids and balance beams for older residents, to provide shared spaces where different ages interact. When we advisers fly in from different countries, we’re starry-eyed at what they can do. Singapore can do things like this in part because they’re smaller, and their government can act quickly. For example, the government recognized about a decade ago that people weren’t saving enough for retirement. So they flipped a switch and noted, “OK, everybody’s putting in more money into their retirement account.”.

Sources indicate that KB: If you had to give a grade to where the U.S. is in implementing the Fresh Map of Life principles, could you take out your red pen?

Recent findings suggest that LC: Compared to some countries, like Singapore, I’d give the U.S. a C-minus, and I am used to grade inflation! The federal government has done little to improve longevity. Unlike the Singapore government, which can require people to save more for retirement, for example, the U.S. cannot rapidly implement such programs. On the other hand, in part because the government contributes less, we see a lot of innovation coming from the private sector. We have entire industries offering new products and services. So I’m optimistic about what the U.S. can contribute to longevity. At a global level, it’s fabulous to think about the different approaches that can come from the public and private sectors in a range of countries.

KB: Longevity has gone mainstream and led to billions of dollars in market interest. How has that changed the center’s work?

LC: It’s true that vast investments are going to longevity. Most of these funds are directed at ways that individuals can live longer. There isn’t, in my experience, much philanthropic interest in this space aimed at helping people live better as we live longer lives. I am discouraged that we are sleepwalking through this seismic demographic shift without investing more in the opportunity to rewrite the life scripts that have guided life and imagining ways that we could use them to improve life.

According to recent reports, it’s also discouraging that as longevity has entered public consciousness, much of what we hear about are pitches for questionable products that supposedly make people live longer. There are so many snake-oil salesmen in this space that it’s hard for consumers to distinguish what is evidence-based and what is not.

Sources indicate that KB: As you often say, transitions are a feature of longer lives. What’s happening next for you?

Sources indicate that LC: I’m going to focus more on research and teaching, but first I’m going on sabbatical and look forward to having more time for the things I love—my garden, being at home, sitting in the sun, going for walks. I want to take Pilates lessons. I’m going to take a break in my schedule to say, “How do I create a healthy lifestyle going forward and build the rest around it?”.

While I hopefully will have a more relaxed schedule, during my sabbatical I’ll be developing an online course called The Fundamentals of Longevity, which will tell the story of longevity and the potential to live longer, better lives, a change we really need in the world. The course will be accessible far beyond Stanford, so that we can help frame the conversation around longevity and help people appreciate the extraordinary promise of science, technology, and social change to improve life. There is a crisis on the horizon if we don’t change the way we live.

We have the opportunity to change our lives for the better. We have opportunities no previous generation of humans in history has had, and we need to start implementing them.

  • Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.

Of the six types of clothing the researchers compared, track pants also received the lowest average ratings for trustworthiness.

Blouses topped the rankings for intelligence and trustworthiness but scored near the bottom for confidence.

Short skirts highlighted almost the reverse pattern, scoring near the top for confidence and lower than long skirts on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Short skirts also gave the strongest impression of sexual interest, showing how much people can read into a hemline.

Long skirts fell between short skirts and blouses on confidence, while ordinary trousers scored higher than tracksuit bottoms on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Onesies gave the strongest impression of happiness and scored about as high as short skirts for confidence.

White clothes suggested a happier wearer than grey clothes did, with black clothes coming last.

These examples show how the impression changes with the question being asked: a blouse came out ahead for intelligence, while a onesie came out ahead for happiness.

The researchers began by asking about 200 people what they thought clothes could tell them about someone and comparing their answers with traits examined in previous research.

They then gathered ratings on 5,000 photographs from online shops, covering five kinds of impressions: intelligence, confidence, trustworthiness, happiness and sexual interest.

Participants formed these impressions from photographs of the garments alone, without seeing anyone wearing them.

The results indicated that who was doing the judging explained more of the variation in ratings than which garment they saw.

For example, one person might associate tracksuit bottoms with training for a race, while another might picture someone spending a Sunday on the sofa.

The researchers draw a parallel between judging people by their clothes and judging them by their faces:.

“That is, much like inferences from faces, the inferred attributes often lie in the eye of the beholder.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Computational Social Science (Rosenbusch et al., 2021).
